The analysis used the STAN5 two-dimensional boundary layer code to match the heat transfer data and extract transition information.
Transition starting points were found to be located well ahead of the minimum heat transfer point in many cases.
Momentum thickness Reynolds numbers at the start of transition ranged from 74 to 400, while at the end of transition they ranged from 330 to 1620.
Higher free stream turbulence levels were found to cause earlier transition and shorter transition lengths.
Stronger flow acceleration, characterized by higher values of the acceleration parameter K, resulted in significantly longer transition regions.
The highest free stream turbulence intensity among the cases analyzed was 18.7%.
The analysis did not explicitly account for local effects of pressure gradient or turbulence within the transition region.
The fully laminar and fully turbulent STAN5 calculations provided the upper and lower bounds for the transitional boundary layer results.
The datasets analyzed covered a wide range of conditions, from low-speed flat plates to high-speed turbine airfoils.
The results indicate that free stream turbulence and pressure gradient have strong, opposite effects on transition location and length.
Transition starting points were often located very close to the leading edge stagnation point, especially for the turbine vane cases.
For the higher turbulence turbine vane case, the calculated boundary layer never fully reached a turbulent state.
The transient combustion-heated turbine vane case exhibited the highest free stream turbulence and strongest flow acceleration.
The analysis tabulated the derived transition start and end locations in terms of momentum thickness Reynolds number for each case.
The datasets included both incompressible flat plate tests and high-speed turbine airfoil tests with compressible flow.
